source.title: An Atari Model Zoo for Analyzing, Visualizing, and Comparing Deep Reinforcement Learning Agents
source.authors: F. Such; Vashisht Madhavan; Rosanne Liu; Rui Wang; P. S. Castro; Yulun Li; Jiale Zhi; Ludwig Schubert; Marc G. Bellemare; J. Clune; J. Lehman

record.tranche_reason: The paper qualitatively compares visualized neuron features across trained models, but does not measure representational alignment or use a convergence-distance metric.
record.gate_note: The feature visualizations in Figures S13–S15 bear on whether features recur across models. The policy-state classifier and RAM-state t-SNE compare policies or visited states, not model representations; the paper also says high-level DNN embeddings are separate for each model. Those results are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: A tools paper, but its qualitative visualizations compare learned features across DRL algorithms on Atari, a new setting. Examples: first-layer edge-like filters, a submarine-detecting neuron, and DQN vs Rainbow synthetic inputs. These results bear only on V5, and only qualitatively.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors present the zoo and software as a platform. Their initial analyses highlight distinctions between DRL algorithm families (gradient-based vs evolutionary filters, robustness, policy distinctiveness), not shared representations. They call for more systematic visualization work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses activation maximization and qualitative neuron visualization, rather than a representation-alignment method or similarity-distance comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Game, layer, and selected neurons vary across visualizations; the authors note that regularization choices were adjusted by hand for some images.

fits_no_version.finding: A2C, ES and GA converge to the same sub-optimal Seaquest behaviour across all runs. This shows up in frame-classifier confusion and in a shared RAM t-SNE embedding.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different RL algorithms converge to similar policies or visited-state distributions (behavioural, not representational, convergence).

record.peer_reviewed: International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence
record.problems: The cross-model feature evidence is qualitative and limited to selected neurons and representative runs. The paper does not quantify feature correspondence or test how consistently features recur across models or seeds.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results left out. The policy classifier and state-space visualizations concern policy behavior or visited states rather than representational alignment.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep; no alignment metric.
No cross-modal models or paired data.
Independent runs exist, but their features are not compared across seeds.
No mapping, stitching or transfer between models.
No quantitative feature matching, no circuits, no SAE features, and no systematic cross-seed recurrence.
No test of alignment level or its causes.

missing.what: First-layer filters across 7 algorithms: edge-detector-like filters sometimes appear in gradient-based methods, never as crisp as in vision models, and are less regular in evolutionary methods. Filters look random when learning fails.
A submarine-detecting third-conv neuron was found in Ape-X; no such specialized neuron was found for ES or GA, whose activations look more distributed.
Rainbow's first output neuron shows interpretable features (submarine, seabed); DQN's Q-value outputs did not.
In Freeway, one Rainbow fully-connected neuron captures lane features; nothing comparable is reported for DQN.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence for V5 is weak: qualitative visualizations of selected neurons from single representative runs, with hand-tuned regularization. The paper's emphasis is on differences between algorithm families, which limits V5 more than it supports it. The DQN/Rainbow comparisons involve closely related value-based variants trained on the same game. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No scale or capability sweep and no measurement of representation alignment across differently trained models.
No paired image-caption data or cross-modal models.
Although the study includes independent runs, it does not compare their learned features or shared subspaces across seeds.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment test.

Only qualitative visual comparisons of selected neurons in representative DQN and Rainbow runs; no systematic test of feature identity, circuits, or recurrence across seeds and broader model families.
No comparison of representation-similarity metrics, their settings, or input-distribution choices.
No test of whether representation alignment plateaus or is explained by shared data or objectives.

rows.subject: DQN
rows.operation_detail: Optimized synthetic inputs to activate selected neurons.
rows.measure: Qualitative features shown by activation-maximizing synthetic inputs.
rows.value: The selected neurons appear to learn edge-detector-style features.
rows.locator: Supplementary Figure S13 and section S2.2
rows.note: The caption describes the visualizations for representative DQN and Rainbow runs as appearing to show edge-detector-style features; this row records the DQN side of that qualitative comparison.
rows.check: The edge-detector-style first-layer features appear in both DQN and Rainbow (Fig S13), so the recurrence holds qualitatively. 'Partial' understates it. The evidence is still visual only.

relationships.condition: Gradient-based vs evolutionary algorithms (ES, GA), and Rainbow vs DQN output layer
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not the rows. Edge-like filters appear in gradient-based methods but are less regular in evolutionary ones. No submarine neuron was found for ES/GA. Rainbow's output features are interpretable but DQN's are not (Sec 4.1, 5.1, Fig 4).
relationships.display_finding: Evolutionary methods had less regular edge-like filters and no identified submarine neuron, while output features were interpretable in Rainbow but not DQN.

relation.reason: Its own cross-agent visualizations bear on V5, despite the paper's primary purpose being a model zoo and analysis toolkit.

tranche.reason: The paper reports qualitative results bearing on recurring features in the new setting of Atari reinforcement-learning agents.

source_check.notes: Evidence concerns selected qualitative visualizations, without quantified feature correspondence. Figure 4 compares different output objectives: Rainbow's C51 low-return probability and DQN Q-values.

statements.correction: Figure S14: shared broad object and animation-related feature categories; individual-feature correspondence untested. Section 4.1: evolutionary filters less regular. Section 5.1: submarine detector found in Ape-X, none found in ES or GA. Figure 4: interpretable Rainbow output visualization; comparable interpretability not observed when maximizing or minimizing DQN Q-value outputs.
statements.problem: The descriptive comparisons are accurate, but absence of demonstrated individual-feature correspondence in Figure S14 does not establish a scope limitation. The algorithm and output-layer differences do provide separate qualifying evidence.

reader_labels.reason: The figures suggest some broad qualitative feature resemblance, but the evidence is visual and limited to selected neurons and representative runs; it does not demonstrate that the same features or circuits recur. Rows r1–r6.
